Yes—there are real disconnects in the current implementation. The main issue is that **settings, push routing, checkpoint reads, `status`, and `doctor` do not share one complete destination resolver**.

I inspected the checkout and merged history without changing files or pushing anything.

One important caveat: your installed CLI is `0.10.1-nightly.202608180612.e2de3d346` from August 18, while this checkout is from August 25 and contains later fixes. Its live output is therefore not a reliable test of this checkout.

### How remote selection currently works

Two similarly named settings control different things:

| Setting under `strategy_options` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"checkpoint_push_remote": "upstream"` | Choose a configured Git remote that carries checkpoints. |
| `"checkpoint_remote": {"provider":"github","repo":"org/checkpoints"}` | Route checkpoints to a separate repository using a derived URL. |
| `"push_sessions": false` | Disable automatic checkpoint pushes. |

The local settings layer overrides project settings **by strategy-option key**. A local `checkpoint_remote` replaces that whole object.

For ordinary named remotes, selection follows:

1. Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote`.
2. A previously observed and saved checkpoint destination.
3. `origin`.
4. The sole remote, or the first configured remote.

An explicit nonexistent remote disables checkpoint syncing. A push to another remote normally sends code without checkpoints. Automatic selection can move after a qualifying push delivers checkpoints, but it does not follow every subsequent branch or push.

Crucially, setting `checkpoint_push_remote` does **not** mean “whenever I push code anywhere, separately push checkpoints to this remote.” It determines which code pushes are allowed to carry checkpoints.

A successfully resolved **dedicated `checkpoint_remote` bypasses that restriction**. See [checkpoint_sync_remote.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:43).

### Where the behavior disconnects

**1. A configured dedicated repository can deliberately be ignored.**

For a `checkpoint_remote` in tracked `settings.json`, the current ownership guard checks both `origin` and every push URL. An owner mismatch—or an owner it cannot determine—makes the setting look inherited from upstream.

That disables dedicated routing for that push; the normal single-remote gate then applies. Putting the setting in an untracked `settings.local.json` establishes explicit local intent and bypasses the ownership heuristic.

This explains how a valid setting can appear “not respected.” It is an intentional heuristic, but it also affects legitimate backups or repositories under another organization.

**2. Writes can reject that setting while reads still use it.**

The fetch resolver does not apply the same ownership check. Consequently, writes may go to an elected remote while reads look in the configured dedicated repository.

The commit introducing the latest ownership restriction explicitly calls this out as **“Not addressed.”** This is a confirmed code-path mismatch, although I have not reproduced your particular failure. See [util.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/remote/util.go:194).

**3. `status` predicts one destination, but pushes resolve against the actual push target.**

`status` probes dedicated routing using the elected remote. A push to another remote can produce a different ownership verdict.

It also reports a bad `checkpoint_push_remote` before checking the dedicated-repository exemption—even though the hook may successfully push to the dedicated repository. Both discrepancies are explicitly documented as “accepted divergence” in [status.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/status.go:320).

**4. The doctor destination warning describes topology, not the complete election.**

It examines all remotes and whether each resolves to a dedicated repository. It does not use `checkpoint_push_remote` to decide that an otherwise ambiguous topology has been explicitly resolved.

So the warning can remain after you have selected a checkpoint remote. Its advice also emphasizes `checkpoint_remote`, despite the named-remote setting being a different legitimate solution.

**5. Checkpoint refs are tracked for one delivery destination.**

The refs backend’s queue records refs without per-destination delivery state. For a remote with multiple push URLs, it pushes checkpoints to the **first URL only**. The older branch backend retains Git’s fan-out behavior.

That also means an empty queue is not proof that checkpoints exist on every remote—or on a newly selected destination.

### Merged PR history

These are the directly relevant merged changes I found:

| PR | Relevance |
|---|---|
| [#677](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/677) | Original separate checkpoint-remote support. |
| [#798](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/798) | Exposed checkpoint-remote configuration through `configure`. |
| [#976](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/976), [#989](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/989), [#995](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/995) | Checkpoint-remote reads and shared remote-resolution infrastructure. |
| [#1279](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1279), [#1732](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1732) | Provider fallback and `entire://` mirror routing. |
| [#1719](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1719) | Bootstrap from the configured checkpoint repository instead of an empty orphan. |
| [#1893](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1893) | Single elected checkpoint remote, explicit setting, and sync reporting. |
| [#1897](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1897), [#1905](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1905) | Multi-push-URL tests, first-destination refs pushes, and destination warnings. |
| [#1898](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1898) | Changed dedicated-repository ownership detection to use origin. |
| [#1951](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1951) | Reads follow the elected remote, with origin as a legacy read fallback. |
| [#1956](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1956) | Discover remote checkpoint refs without a dedicated repository. |
| [#1987](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1987) | Explain skipped checkpoint syncing when checkpoints are waiting. |
| [#1991](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1991) | Automatically capture the checkpoint destination from qualifying pushes. |
| [#2036](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2036) | Require confirmed delivery before capture; reintroduce push-destination ownership checks; correct doctor wording. |
| [#2086](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2086) | Related: trail branches respect their push remote instead of hardcoded origin. |

GitHub search succeeded once but subsequent requests repeatedly timed out, so I cannot honestly call this exhaustive. The checkpoint transcript lookup also failed with `ref file is empty`; the findings above come from source, commit messages, and merge history.

content.text:
[#2327](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2327) directly addresses several issues we identified. It is currently **open, not merged**.

It adds three substantial changes:

- **Correct configuration advice:** doctor and multi-URL warnings now distinguish `checkpoint_push_remote` (a remote name) from `checkpoint_remote` (a dedicated repository object).
- **Automatic Entire destination:** a single qualifying `entire://` remote becomes preferred over `origin`. Every code push then sends checkpoints there, even when pushing code elsewhere.
- **Explicit backlog migration:** `entire checkpoint migrate` republishes existing checkpoints, verifies delivery, and optionally removes old copies with separate consent. Status gains migration reporting.

However, the diff reveals an important remaining inconsistency: **automatic selection and explicit configuration of the same Entire remote behave differently.**

| Selection of the Entire remote | Checkpoints accompany pushes to other remotes? |
|---|---|
| Automatically selected through the new `entire` tier | Yes |
| Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote` setting | No—the ordinary gate still applies |
| Previously captured destination | No—the ordinary gate still applies |

The redirect checks `elected.Source == SyncRemoteSourceEntire`, rather than whether the selected destination is an Entire remote. Explicit settings outrank that tier and return source `config`. Consequently, explicitly selecting the destination can disable the behavior automatic selection provides. Doctor’s new “destination settled” handling also only recognizes source `entire`. [Relevant diff](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2327/files)

Two other limitations matter for your setup:

- Your `origin` has a GitHub fetch URL and an `entire://` push URL. The new detection requires **every fetch and push URL** to be `entire://`, so that mixed remote does not qualify.
- Successfully resolved dedicated `checkpoint_remote` routing still takes precedence. This PR does not unify its ownership checks, read routing, and status prediction.

So this is highly relevant work, particularly for misleading advice and stranded historical checkpoints. But it also gives us a concrete case to investigate next: **why explicitly choosing a remote changes delivery semantics compared with automatically choosing that exact same remote.** This conclusion is from inspecting the diff; I haven’t run its tests.

See the images on desktop remote_wrong and settings_remote. Also, when they ran entire status they got, failed to load settings: loading settings: reading settings file: parsing settings file: json: unknown field "checkpoint_remote"

I’ll inspect the two Desktop images and check how the settings parser handles the suggested configuration. That error suggests `checkpoint_remote` was placed at the top level, while both remote settings belong under `strategy_options`.

content.text:
The screenshots confirm the failure chain: **the CLI’s advice led the user to an invalid configuration.**

`remote_wrong.png` tells them to set `checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.json`, without showing its structure. They reasonably added:

```json
"checkpoint_remote": "entire"
```

`settings_remote.png` shows that at the top level. There are two problems:

- **Wrong location:** the settings parser rejects unknown top-level fields, causing `entire status` to fail entirely.
- **Wrong setting:** choosing the Git remote named `entire` requires `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`. Merely moving `"checkpoint_remote": "entire"` under `strategy_options` would stop that parsing error but silently ignore the string—it expects a repository object.

The correct configuration is to remove the invalid top-level entry, preserve their other project settings, and add this to `.entire/settings.local.json`:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "checkpoint_push_remote": "entire"
  }
}
```

Using the local file keeps a clone-specific remote name out of teammates’ configuration. The setting also works under `strategy_options` in project `settings.json`; that file itself is not the cause of the error.

This strengthens the case for #2327’s wording fix, but we should also cover **recovery from the already-broken configuration**. Better advice alone will not repair those files. The parser should ideally explain the correct key and nesting when it encounters this particular mistake.

And the earlier #2327 concern applies directly here: explicitly setting `"checkpoint_push_remote": "entire"` selects source `config`, so the proposed automatic Entire redirect does not apply. Pushing to `entire` can carry checkpoints; pushing code to `origin` still skips them. That needs to be reconciled with the intended behavior.
so 2327 also takes care of working fix?

Partly. #2327 includes working behavior changes, not just corrected wording: it automatically selects a sole qualifying Entire remote, redirects checkpoint pushes there, and adds backlog migration.

But it does **not fully fix the reported scenario**:

- Existing invalid `"checkpoint_remote": "entire"` settings still need correction.
- Explicitly setting `checkpoint_push_remote: "entire"` bypasses the new automatic tier, so pushes to `origin` still won’t send checkpoints to `entire`.
- The dedicated-repository read/write inconsistencies remain.

So I would call it a substantial partial fix, not complete resolution. It’s still open, and my assessment is from the diff—not a tested verification.
i meant wording fix

Yes—#2327 fixes the wording in both the enable/doctor remote note and the multi-URL push warning. It points users to `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json` and distinguishes that from the dedicated-repository `checkpoint_remote` setting.
okay so what else needs fixing?

Beyond #2327’s wording fix, I’d prioritize these:

1. **Make explicit and automatic selection behave consistently.** In #2327, automatically selecting an Entire remote sends checkpoints there on every code push. Explicitly selecting that same remote with `checkpoint_push_remote` disables that redirect. This is the clearest remaining behavior issue.

2. **Unify push routing, reads, status, and doctor.** A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` can be rejected by the push-side ownership check while reads still use it. Status can report a destination that a particular push won’t use, and doctor can warn about ambiguity despite an explicit selection. They need a shared resolution result, including why a setting was ignored.

3. **Make configuration errors actionable.** Top-level `checkpoint_remote` should explain the required nesting. A string under `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote` should produce a clear validation error instead of being silently ignored. Already-broken files need useful recovery guidance.

4. **Handle destination changes and historical checkpoints consistently.** Changing the selected remote does not republish refs already removed from the push queue. #2327 adds migration, but status should distinguish “nothing queued” from “all checkpoints verified at this destination,” including explicitly selected destinations.

5. **Clarify mixed fetch/push URL support.** Your GitHub-fetch / Entire-push `origin` does not qualify for #2327’s automatic Entire tier. We should establish the intended behavior for that common setup and make the reporting match it.

I’d tackle **1 and 2 first**, then validate the combined behavior across explicit settings, automatic selection, dedicated repositories, and mixed URLs. These are findings from the source and PR diff; they still need focused reproduction before implementation.
does 1 and 2 depend on 2327?

**1 depends on #2327.** The explicit-versus-automatic inconsistency comes from its new Entire selection tier. Ideally, fix it within that PR before merging.

**2 mostly does not.** The dedicated-repository read/write mismatch and status/doctor inconsistencies already exist in the current code. They can be fixed independently, but should account for #2327’s new routing behavior to avoid creating another divergence.
okay how would we do 2?

I’d introduce one shared **checkpoint routing resolver**, then make push, reads, `status`, and `doctor` consume its result.

Today, the named-remote election and dedicated-repository resolution happen separately, with callers deciding precedence and fallback behavior. That’s where they disagree.

The resolver should return:

- The configured destination and which setting selected it.
- The effective write destination.
- Whether syncing is enabled, disabled, or waiting for a push to the selected remote.
- Why a dedicated setting was rejected or could not resolve.
- Read destinations, distinguishing the active store from historical fallbacks.

There’s one important distinction to preserve: **status describes configuration; the hook evaluates a specific push.** We shouldn’t make status guess which remote the next push will target. They should share the same rules, with the hook supplying the actual push target.

For example, status could say:

```text
Checkpoints: upstream (set by checkpoint_push_remote)
Syncs when pushing to upstream.
Dedicated repository org/checkpoints ignored: ownership mismatch.
```

Then I’d update the consumers:

| Consumer | Change |
|---|---|
| Push hook | Use the resolved destination and eligibility directly. |
| Reads | Look in the effective checkpoint store first; retain appropriate historical fallbacks. |
| Status | Show the selection, conditions, and rejection reasons. Keep it network-free. |
| Doctor | Diagnose unresolved configuration; stop treating multiple remotes alone as ambiguity. |

The tricky case is ownership rejection: if writes go to a fork, reads should search that fork first. The inherited dedicated repository might still contain useful upstream history, so I wouldn’t simply remove it from all reads—but it must not remain the assumed authoritative write destination.

I’d implement this in two stages:

1. Extract the shared resolution without changing behavior.
2. Correct the disagreements with focused regression tests: ownership mismatch, explicit non-origin selection, invalid named remote alongside a dedicated repository, and different fetch/push URLs.

That can start independently of #2327. Its Entire redirect would then become another explicit rule in the shared resolver, rather than a separate exception each command has to understand.
why do you need to create a resolver, when the remote should be consistent already

You’re right—we already have `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` and the dedicated-repository URL helpers. I jumped too quickly to a new abstraction.

The issue is that callers use those existing pieces differently:

- Push checks dedicated routing before applying the named-remote gate.
- Status checks the named-remote election first.
- Reads don’t apply the same dedicated-repository ownership decision.
- Doctor evaluates remote topology without fully respecting the selected destination.

We should trace those call sites and fix the inconsistent precedence and interpretation using the existing helpers. Extract shared logic only where necessary to prevent the same decision being implemented differently again.

The remote should stay consistent; the first task is identifying exactly where each consumer stops honoring that decision.

Yes. The trace shows the existing election generally honors a valid `checkpoint_push_remote`. The inaccuracies arise **after election**, when callers apply different checks or interpret the result differently.

I built this checkout and reproduced status output in isolated temporary repositories. No project files or remote refs were changed.

### Confirmed inconsistencies

| Case | What happens | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `push_sessions: false` | Status still says “Checkpoints sync to: upstream.” The hook skips automatic checkpoint pushes. | Status checks whether Entire is enabled, but never checks whether checkpoint pushing is disabled. |
| Missing `checkpoint_push_remote` plus valid dedicated repository | Status says “Checkpoints NOT syncing.” The hook can still use the dedicated repository. | Status returns the election error first; the hook resolves dedicated routing first and bypasses election when successful. |
| Dedicated setting rejected because of ownership | Pushes can target the elected fork, but discovery and blob reads still target the dedicated repository. | Reads check whether the setting **exists**, not whether push routing accepted it. |
| Explicitly selected remote among several remotes | Doctor/enable can still call the destination ambiguous. | Their ambiguity calculation counts unpinned remotes without consulting the explicit election. |
| Different fetch and push URLs | Reads and writes can reach different repositories while status displays the same remote name. | Readers resolve the fetch URL; writers use push URLs. The remote name hides that distinction. |

### The most consequential call-site mismatch

For a configuration with:

```text
origin: acme/app
fork: contributor/app
checkpoint_push_remote: fork
checkpoint_remote: acme/checkpoints
```

The paths disagree:

- **Push:** `prePush` → `resolvePushSettings` → `PushURL` rejects the dedicated repository on ownership grounds → the election permits `fork`.
- **Status:** reports `fork`, which I reproduced.
- **Discovery:** `listCheckpointRefsOnRemote` sees a valid dedicated setting → queries `acme/checkpoints` → returns without trying the elected fork.
- **Blob hydration:** `checkpointBlobFetchTargets` likewise selects only the dedicated target.

So this is more than misleading wording: **a checkpoint can be published to a destination that subsequent discovery does not search.**

The decisive short-circuits are in [git_operations.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/git_operations.go:636) and [checkpointBlobFetchTargets](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/git_operations.go:812).

### Two additional reporting limitations

**Doctor’s metadata check does not establish checkpoint-ref delivery.** It examines locally available tracking branches. With the refs backend, it skips that comparison and prints “OK” because the primary is not a pushed branch. With a dedicated branch store, its tracking-ref selection still follows named remotes and can inspect stale origin metadata instead of the dedicated store. See [doctor.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/doctor.go:464).

**The refs “unpushed” count is not destination-specific.** `CountUnpushedCheckpoints` ignores its remote argument for the refs backend and returns the shared queue length. Changing destinations does not make previously delivered refs appear in that count. See [unpushed_checkpoints.go](/Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents%20-%20Peyton’s%20MacBook%20Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/origin/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/unpushed_checkpoints.go:21).

My earlier description also needs one qualification: status using the elected remote while the hook uses the actual push target is not inherently wrong. The inaccurate part is presenting that conditional result as an unconditional “syncs to” statement.

The first fixes should address the **read-path short-circuits**, **status’s missing disabled check and reversed precedence**, and **doctor’s failure to respect explicit election**. None requires introducing a new resolver. The runtime checks verified the status outputs; the push/read disagreements above are confirmed from the call paths, not live remote delivery tests.

**The basic non-origin selection works.** These cases successfully delivered and discovered the checkpoint on `fork`:

- Explicit `checkpoint_push_remote: "fork"`.

The problematic or surprising cases were:

| Case | Reproduced behavior |
|---|---|
| **Selected fork has different fetch/push URLs** | Checkpoint reaches the push destination; queue empties; discovery returns **0** because it reads the fetch destination. |
| **Push directly to the selected fork’s URL** | No checkpoint delivery; queue retains **1**. Pushing by remote name works. The gate compares names, not equivalent destinations. |
| **Select fork, then push code to origin** | No checkpoint delivery anywhere; queue retains **1**. Explicit selection is a gate, not an instruction to independently push checkpoints to the fork. |
| **Selected fork has two push URLs** | Only the first receives the checkpoint. Discovery succeeds when its fetch URL matches that first destination; the second receives nothing. |
| **Rename the explicitly selected fork** | Sync stops and status correctly reports the stale setting. The setting does not follow Git remote renames. |

Combined with the earlier reproduction, the strongest failures affecting non-origin users are:

1. **Split fetch/push destinations:** successful delivery followed by failed discovery.
2. **Inherited dedicated settings:** they override discovery even after ownership checks reject them for pushing.
3. **Misleading expectations around explicit selection:** users may expect every code push to sync to their selected fork, but the implementation only permits checkpoint delivery when that remote is pushed.

The evidence does **not** support a general claim that `checkpoint_push_remote` is ignored. The failures depend on the surrounding configuration and push invocation.

content.text:
Yes—this is a separate onboarding improvement, and it can be much simpler than migration.

### What `enable` does today

I checked current `main` (`0138471ae`):

1. Sets up or re-enables Entire.
2. Inspects the remotes.
3. Prints the “checkpoint destination ambiguous” note.
4. Leaves the user to edit settings.

The detection already exists, but it’s advisory. It counts multiple unpinned remotes rather than asking the user to resolve the choice. The actual checkpoint election is separate: explicit setting → previously observed selection → origin → sole remote → first remote.

### The PRs were split

| PR | Current scope |
|---|---|
| [#2335](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2335) | Automatic Entire-remote election and corrected settings hints |
| [#2327](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2327) | Moving existing checkpoints and optional cleanup; stacked on #2335 |
| [#1172](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1172) | Older picker: “this repo / separate private repo / local only,” **not named-remote selection** |

All three are open. So there is related picker work to account for, but it doesn’t describe the specific flow you want.

### My recommendation

Add a narrow **named-remote picker to interactive `enable`**, built from main:

```text
Detected 2 Git remotes.
Where should checkpoints be pushed?

  origin   github.com/team/project
❯ fork     github.com/you/project

Checkpoint destination saved: fork
Applies to this clone.
```

Selecting `fork` writes only:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "checkpoint_push_remote": "fork"
  }
}
```

to `.entire/settings.local.json`, preserving other settings.

Reuse the existing topology inspection, remote-election helper, settings writer, and interactive selector patterns. **No new resolver, migration engine, checkpoint copying, or deletion.**

A few boundaries keep it accurate:

- Respect an existing explicit selection or effective dedicated checkpoint repository; don’t overwrite it just because two remotes exist.
- Don’t turn checkpoint pushing back on when `push_sessions` is disabled.
- Skip prompting for `--yes`, targeted `--agent`, and non-interactive execution.
- Keep multi-push-URL warnings separate: choosing a remote doesn’t resolve that remote having several destinations.
- Make the same resolution available on re-running `enable`, not only first setup.

One important wording detail: on current main, selecting `fork` means **pushes to fork carry checkpoints**. It does not make every push to another remote forward checkpoints there. #2335 introduces forwarding for automatically elected Entire remotes; this picker shouldn’t quietly change that policy.

I’d keep this separate from migration and preserve #2335’s automatic Entire selection when it lands. Compared with extending #1172’s broader destination wizard, this is the smaller, more targeted change.

Does that scope—including resolving an unset destination when someone re-runs `enable`—match what you want?

then this would cover 

github
entire 

which is like what was in the split prs right?

Yes—`github` and `entire` would appear as the two named remotes, and the user could choose one. The CLI would save that choice automatically.

The split is:

- **#2335:** automatically prefer the Entire remote when no explicit selection overrides it.
- **This picker:** let the user explicitly select GitHub or Entire during `enable`.
- **#2327:** move previously pushed checkpoints between destinations afterward.

One nuance: #2335 distinguishes **automatically elected Entire** from **explicitly selected remotes** when deciding whether every code push forwards checkpoints. We should check that interaction so choosing `entire` in the picker doesn’t unexpectedly lose the forwarding behavior.
so we should just reuse this?

Yes—reuse the existing remote detection, election, and settings handling. Add only the interactive choice in `enable`.

For `github` + `entire`, we should preserve #2335’s automatic Entire selection and offer the user a chance to change it, rather than unnecessarily writing an explicit override.

That keeps the responsibilities clear: existing code determines the destination; `enable` lets the user confirm or change it; #2327 handles migration separately. We should inspect #1172 for reusable picker code too, without adopting its broader setup flow.
okay so tell me plan again

The plan is a focused `enable` improvement—not migration.

1. **Start from current main.** Check #2335’s latest election behavior and #1172’s picker code for reuse. Don’t pull in #2327’s migration machinery.

2. **Reuse existing detection and election.** Identify the configured remotes and current checkpoint destination. No new resolver.

3. **Offer an interactive choice when multiple destinations need resolution:**

   ```text
   Detected 2 remotes. Where should checkpoints go?

   ❯ entire  — current automatic destination
     github
   ```

   Preserve existing explicit selections, dedicated checkpoint settings, and disabled pushing.

4. **Persist only what’s needed.** Keeping the automatic destination leaves configuration unchanged. Changing it saves `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json`, preserving unrelated settings.

5. **Report the actual result.** Confirm the destination and accurately explain when checkpoints will push. Resolve the choice on first setup or re-running `enable`; skip the picker for non-interactive invocations. Keep multi-URL warnings separate.

6. **Verify compatibility and user flows.** Test GitHub + Entire, origin + fork, existing selections, disabled pushing, cancellation, and non-interactive execution. Specifically verify that selecting Entire preserves the intended forwarding behavior from #2335.

Before implementation, write the detailed plan and run a reviewer over it. Keep migration, copying, and deleting existing checkpoints entirely out of scope.
okay and then it will tell the user in output that after selecting it will output what it did? and then do you have a non interactive option too?

Yes. After selection, it should say **what changed and what that means**, for example:

```text
Checkpoint destination set to: github
Saved to .entire/settings.local.json for this clone.
Checkpoints will be uploaded when you push to github.
```

If they keep the automatic destination:

```text
Keeping checkpoint destination: entire (automatic).
No settings changed.
```

For non-interactive use, I’d add:

```bash
entire enable --yes --checkpoint-push-remote github
```

That explicitly selects the remote, validates it exists, saves the same local setting, and prints the same confirmation. An invalid remote should fail before setup changes anything.

`--yes` alone should **preserve existing/default behavior**, not silently choose a new destination. This would be a proposed new flag; `--checkpoint-remote` remains the separate dedicated-repository option.
okay proceed wiht writing plan then

I’ll write the plan with the interactive confirmation output and explicit non-interactive flag, then have it reviewed. I’ll keep the #2335 compatibility questions explicit and leave migration out of scope.

+
+| State | Interactive enable | Without interaction |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Multiple remotes, no explicit/dedicated selection, pushing enabled | Offer current choice plus other eligible named remotes | Preserve election; show current result and explicit-flag hint |
+| Valid explicit selection | Preserve and report; no repeated picker | Same |
+| Effective dedicated checkpoint store | Preserve and report actual dedicated destination; no misleading named-remote picker | Same |
+| Pushing disabled | No picker; report disabled | Same |
+| No remotes or one remote | No picker; preserve current no-remote/sole-remote behavior | Same |
+| Explicit remote flag | Validate and pin requested named remote; bypass picker | Same |
+| Invalid existing explicit remote | Offer repair from eligible remotes if interactive and pushing enabled; keep-current means no repair and a truthful warning | Preserve fail-closed behavior; provide flag-based repair hint |
+| Cancel/Escape | Abort enable before new setup writes; no destination change | Not applicable |

+An explicit flag with disabled pushing stores the future destination but MUST NOT enable pushing; confirmation states that pushing remains disabled. `--checkpoint-push-remote` and `--checkpoint-remote` together are rejected before writes. With an existing effective dedicated setting, reject a flag selection if `remote.PushURL(ctx, candidate)` still resolves to the dedicated store: explain that the flag cannot replace that separate setting, and change nothing. Do not remove dedicated configuration. A shared inherited dedicated setting rejected by existing ownership checks is not effective and must not suppress the fork picker.

+For a remote with multiple push URLs, keep the backend-specific warning; naming that remote does not repair fan-out. Preserve ordinary selection behavior rather than inventing URL selection. Redact URLs with existing `gitremote.RedactURLOrPath`; do not expose credentials.

+On main, naming a remote `entire` does not grant special forwarding. Do not reproduce #2335's election logic here.

+With #2335 present, retaining the currently automatic Entire selection must be a no-op (no explicit override), preserving automatic forwarding on pushes to other remotes. Selecting another remote or supplying the explicit flag pins it under the existing explicit-tier semantics. Choosing an Entire remote when it is NOT already automatically elected likewise pins it; do not claim this grants automatic-tier forwarding. If product requirements demand identical forwarding for all explicit Entire selections, surface that as separate election-policy work, not a hidden change in this picker.
+

+```text
+Detected 2 Git remotes. Where should checkpoints go?
+> Keep current: entire (automatic) — <redacted destination>
+  github — <redacted destination>

+Keeping checkpoint destination: entire (automatic).
+No checkpoint destination settings changed.
+```

+```text
+Checkpoint destination set to: github
+Saved to .entire/settings.local.json for this clone.
+Checkpoints will be uploaded when you push to github.
+```
+
+If the flag reaffirms an already identical explicit override, report already configured rather than claiming a new write. If disabled, replace the upload promise with `Checkpoint pushing remains disabled.` Only report all-code-push forwarding when existing policy actually enables it. “No settings changed” must be scoped to the destination, since enable can still update hooks and other settings.

+
+When several remotes need a choice, interactive `entire enable` offers a remote
+picker, including when you re-run it in an enabled repository. Keeping the current
+destination leaves its selection unchanged. Choosing another remote saves

+teammates do not inherit a remote name specific to your clone. Existing explicit
+selections and effective dedicated checkpoint repositories are preserved.
+
+To select a remote without the picker:
+
+```bash
+entire enable --yes --checkpoint-push-remote fork

+
+The remote must already exist. An explicit flag pins the named remote, even if
+it is currently selected automatically. `--yes` alone does not change the
+checkpoint destination. The command confirms the effective destination and any
+local settings write. Selecting a destination does not re-enable disabled
+checkpoint pushing, upload existing checkpoints immediately, or move or delete
+checkpoint history from other remotes.
